# Inlining copies the argument to wherever the parameter is read, so a parameter
# read twice evaluates its argument twice. That is the argument's problem and
# not the function's — `double(x) => x + x` is as pure as they come, and
# `double(bump())` counted by two.
#
# Purity of the *callee* was the only condition, which is the wrong side of the
# call: it permitted this, and forbade inlining a readonly function whose
# argument was a literal.

sngl generate --lang go --platform bubbletea --out out app.sngl

# The effect happens once. Either the call is kept or the argument is bound —
# what may not happen is two bumps where the program wrote one.
! grep 'bump\(\).*bump\(\)' out/model.go
grep 'Double\(m\.bump\(\)\)' out/model.go

-- app.sngl --
import . "sngl:ui"
import . "sngl:app"

func double(x int) => x + x

component main {
    var n = 0

    func bump() int {
        n = n + 1
        return n
    }

    window(title="once") {
        text(value=string(double(bump())))
    }
}

output(lang="go", platform="bubbletea")
